speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to your consultation. I see you have a history of episodes involving unresponsiveness and facial grimacing; to understand the underlying cause, please describe what happens during these spells, how long they last, and if you have any history of seizures or fainting.

speaker: Patient
text: 7-year-old boy. The patient has been experiencing recurrent episodes lasting 3–4 minutes each of facial grimacing and staring over the past month. During these episodes, he is nonresponsive and does not recall them afterward. He reports a muddy taste in his mouth before the onset of these episodes. His brother witnessed him waking up, staring, and making hand gestures during one episode. The patient felt lethargic and confused afterwards.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Cataplexy secondary to Narcolepsy Type 1 (Narcolepsy with Cataplexy).

*Clinical Reasoning:* The patient is a 7-year-old boy with recurrent episodes of unresponsiveness, staring, and facial grimacing lasting 3–4 minutes, followed by post-ictal lethargy and confusion. Crucially, the presence of a "muddy taste" (gustatory hallucination) and involuntary "hand gestures" during the event strongly suggests cataplexy—a loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotions, often misidentified as a seizure or fainting spell. The combination of cataplexy and sleep-wake disruption is pathognomonic for Narcolepsy Type 1. No further diagnostic questions are needed; the clinical presentation is sufficient for a working diagnosis of Narcolepsy.
